chapters.title: Landmark Foundations I: Niang v. Gonzales and the Asylum Elements
chapters.reason: Niang articulates the Tenth Circuit's formulation of the refugee definition and the three-element past-persecution framework (including the government 'unable or unwilling' prong). Direct excerpts are needed so the chapter can teach and quote the precise statutory interpretation, element language, and burden-shifting guidance from the opinion.

chapters.title: Landmark Foundations II: Rivera-Barrientos and Dallakoti on Nexus and 9One Central Reason9
chapters.reason: Rivera-Barrientos and Dallakoti set out the 'one central reason'/mixed-motive nexus test and key language on incidental or tangential motives. Quoting the cases is important to show the exact standard courts apply and sample application language for nexus analysis.

chapters.title: Landmark Foundations III: Wiransane and Karki on the Persecution Threshold and Threats
chapters.reason: Wiransane and Karki define the persecution threshold and the threats-only rule (and its limits). The chapter benefits from verbatim excerpts to demonstrate how the Tenth Circuit distinguishes mere harassment/threats from legally cognizable persecution and the reasoning used in cumulative-harm analyses.

chapters.title: Landmark Foundations IV: Singh v. Bondi on State Protection, Reporting, and Futility
chapters.reason: Singh clarifies the 'unable or unwilling' state-protection inquiry and the futility/danger exceptions to reporting. Including portions of the opinion will let the chapter present the controlling tests and illustrative factual applications as authoritative source text.
